description: Calcium compounds, silica, alumina and iron oxide are placed in rotating kiln at 1500C.

Cement composed of magnesium oxide and hydrated magnesium carbonates. Produced at lower temperature (180C vs 1250C) and pressure to reduce combustion emissions, as well as allow for biofuel substitution. Absorbs more CO2 than is produced during the process, leading to an absorption of ~100kg CO2 per tonne cement produced. Product is air permeable.
cost: Magnesium is not very common on land, making this option more expensive
reference-type: Survey academic article covering novel methods of cement production.

description: Cement production that mimics coral reefs. CO2-rich flue gas is filtered through seawater. Calcium and magnesium are stripped from seawater to create cement as strong as OPC, and air permeable (potential building efficiency benefits). Similar product to Novacem but different process.
ghg-impact: Essentially would be carbon neutral, as carbon comes from recycled effluent
reference-type: Survey academic article covering novel methods of cement production.

description: Aluminum-silicon based cement, made from sand, water, natural or synthetic pozzolans and an alkali activator. Competitive in terms of cost with OPC as well as strength.
reference-type: Survey academic article covering novel methods of cement production.

description: Produced in a reactor by rapid calcination of dolomitic rock in superheated steam.

C-Fix was developed by Shell and the University of Delft (NL) and needs to be heated to 200°C before being added to aggregates/fillers to make a ´carbon concrete´. It has properties in common with both asphalt and cement-based concretes but is mixed and applied using asphalt techniques.
Utilises waste materials from the power industry (fly ash, bottom ash), the steel industry (slag), and from concrete waste, to make alkali-activated cements.
Increase use of clinker substitutes

description: Pre-reduction and final reduction of iron ore takes place at different levels within the same cyclone, reducing heat losses of different steps. Oxygen and coal (or other biomass) is introduce at the bottom of the cyclone.
energy-impact: 20% reduction in energy consumption (13-14 GJ/tonne hot metal vs 16.1 GJ/tonne hot metal for BF production)
reference-type: Survey peer-reviewed article covering novel methods of Iron and Steel production.

technology-name: Smelt Reduction - Coke free steel making (e.g., COREX, FINEX, ITmk3 and Hismelt)
description: Iron ore udergoes a solid-state reduction in a pre-reduction unit and is then smelted and further reduced in a vessel where coal is gasified.  It combines a number of processes, preheating of coal, partial pyrolysis in a reactor, an ore melting cyclone and a vessel for ore reduction.
ghg-impact: Up to 20% CO2 emission reductions compared to BF-BOF
cost: Estimates are that both capital and operating expenditures would be lower.

description: Pellets of Iron and high-volatility Coal are heated and reduced to 95% metallized pellets suitable for use in an EAF. The product of reduction (CO gas) is released and heated above the bed to drive the process. More efficient than traditional Blast Furnace.
ghg-impact: 33% reduction per t of hot metal produced
cost: $16.7 M for facility producing 46,000 t a year of DRI
reference-type: Survey peer-reviewed article covering novel methods of Iron and Steel production.

description: Gasified coal is used to directly reduce iron ores in a solid-gas moving bed reactor.Oxygen is removed from ores using reactions based on H2 and CO to create highly metallized DRI. Can gasify and use pretty much any carbon-bearing fuel.
reference-type: Survey peer-reviewed article covering novel methods of Iron and Steel production.

description: Most virgin steel is made using the BF-BOF process, while recycled steel is almost entirely produced using an electric arc furnace.  The lower the GHG intensity of electricity, the lower the process GHG intensity.  According to J. Allwood, in most developed coutnires there is sufficent recyclable steel available to meet all needs, but it tends to be contaminated with tin and copper.  If these could be seperated, either through design or labour, the mix of recycled steel in the overall mix could rise.
reference-type: Survey. Document not pee reviewed but based on peer reviewed literature.

technology-name: Top gas recycling blast furnace (TGR - BF).  (e.g., ULCOS)
description: Off gases in the blast furnace are separated so that useful components are recycled back into the furnace and used as a reducing agent and reducing the amount of coke needed in the furnace. In addition, the concept of injecting Oxygen(O2) into the furnace instead of preheated air, removes unwanted Nitrogen(N2) from the gas, facilitating Carbon dioxide(CO2) Capture and Storage (CCS).
ghg-impact: Reduces GHG emissions from blast furnace by about 1/3.  Also can facilitate CCS as CO2 stream is higher concentration.
reference-links: Quader, M. A., Ahmed, S., Ghazilla, R. A. R., Ahmed, S., & Dahari, M. (2015).  A comprehensive review on energy efficient CO2 breakthrough technologies for sustainable green iron and steel manufacturing. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 50, 594-614.

technology-name: Increased use of waste heat from high temperature sources such as molten slag
description: As a by-product during steel making, molten slag and hot exhaust waste gases are the main source of high temperature waste heat energy.  Typically only a small portion of waste heat is recovered.  Heat Exchanger technologies have been developed to recover as much as 65% of BF molten slag heat.  Chemical methods may have even greater heat recovery byt are only in the research and development stage.
ghg-impact: Using heat for electricity generation has potential to reduce onsite GHG emissions
reference-links: Quader, M. A., Ahmed, S., Ghazilla, R. A. R., Ahmed, S., & Dahari, M. (2015).  A comprehensive review on energy efficient CO2 breakthrough technologies for sustainable green iron and steel manufacturing. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 50, 594-614.
